danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: I vinteren 1813 giftede Nikolaj sig med fyrstinde Marja og flyttede til Lysye Gory (Kahle Berge) med sin kone, sin mor og Sonja.
I løbet af fire år havde han betalt al sin resterende gæld uden at sælge nogen af sin kones ejendom, og da han modtog en lille arv ved en fætters død, betalte han også sin gæld til Pierre.

I yderligere tre år, inden 1820, havde han styret sine affærer så godt, at han kunne købe et lille gods, der lå op til Lysye Gory, og forhandlede om at købe Otradnoje tilbage — det var hans kæreste drøm.

Da han var begyndt at drive landbrug af nødvendighed, blev han snart så optaget af det, at det blev hans yndlingsbeskæftigelse og næsten hans eneste. Nikolaj var en jævn landmand: han brød sig ikke om nyskabelser, især ikke de engelske, der dengang var på mode. Han lo ad teoretiske afhandlinger om godsdrift, brød sig ikke om fabrikker, om dyrkning af kostbare afgrøder eller om dyre frøsorter. Han beskæftigede sig overhovedet ikke med ét isoleret led i driften, men havde altid hele godset for øje. Det vigtigste var i hans øjne hverken kvælstoffet i jorden eller ilten i luften, hverken gødningen eller de særlige plove. Det vigtigste var den, der fik kvælstoffet og ilten, gødningen og ploven til at virke: bonden, der gjorde arbejdet. Da Nikolaj først tog fat på driften og begyndte at forstå de forskellige sider af den, var det især den livegne bonde, der optog ham. I bonden så han både et redskab, en mand, der selv kunne bedømme driften, og et mål i sig selv. I begyndelsen iagttog han bønderne og prøvede at forstå, hvad de ville, og hvad de selv fandt godt eller skidt. Han lod, som om han ledede arbejdet og gav ordrer, mens det i virkeligheden var ham, der lærte af dem: hvordan de bar sig ad, hvordan de talte, og hvordan de skelnede mellem godt og skidt. Først da han kendte deres smag og ønsker, kunne tale deres sprog og høre, hvad der lå bag ordene, og følte sig beslægtet med dem, tog han med fast hånd fat på at lede sine livegne, det vil sige gøre sin pligt over for dem. Og Nikolaj opnåede glimrende resultater.

Vejledt af en instinktiv begavelse udpegede han, straks da han overtog godsstyrelsen, ufejlbarligt forvalter, landsbyældste og delegeret — de selvsamme folk, bønderne selv ville have valgt, hvis de havde haft ret til at vælge, og disse poster skiftede aldrig hænder. Længe før han gav sig til at analysere gødningens egenskaber eller sætte sig ind i debet og kredit, som han spottende kaldte det, skaffede han sig rede på, hvor meget kvæg bønderne havde, og søgte på alle måder at øge bestanden. Han holdt bondefamilierne samlet i så store hushold som muligt og lod dem ikke dele sig i mindre gårde. Han var lige hård mod den dovne, den lastefulde og den svage og prøvede at få dem udstødt af landsbyfællesskabet.
Han passede lige så omhyggeligt bøndernes såning og høst af hø og korn som sin egen, og få godsejere fik deres afgrøder sået og høstet så tidligt og så godt eller fik så godt et udbytte som Nikolaj.

Han brød sig ikke om at have med hustyendet at gøre — »dronerne,« som han kaldte dem — og alle sagde, at han forkælede dem med sin slaphed. Når der skulle træffes en beslutning om en hustjener, især hvis en skulle straffes, følte han sig altid ubestemt og rådførte sig med alle i huset; men når det var muligt at sende en tjener til at være soldat i stedet for en bonde, gjorde han det uden mindste tøven. Han følte aldrig nogen ubeslutsomhed i sine afgørelser om bønderne. Han vidste, at enhver bestemmelse ville blive godkendt af det store flertal, snarere end afvist.

Han tillod sig hverken at være hård eller straffe en mand, eller at gøre det let for eller belønne nogen, blot fordi han følte sig tilbøjelig til det. Han kunne ikke have sagt, efter hvilken målestok han afgjorde, hvad han burde eller ikke burde gøre, men målestokken var ganske fast og bestemt i hans eget sind.
Ofte sagde han med ærgrelse over en fejl eller uregelmæssighed: »Hvad kan man stille op med vores russiske bønder?« og forestillede sig, at han ikke kunne udholde dem.
Og dog elskede han »vores russiske bønder« og deres levemåde af hele sin sjæl, og netop derfor havde han forstået og tilegnet sig den ene måde at drive landbrug på, der gav gode resultater.

Grevinde Marja var skinsyg på sin mands lidenskab og ked af, at hun ikke kunne dele den. Men hvad der kunne glæde eller ærgre ham sådan i denne verden, som lå hende så fjernt, begreb hun ikke. Hvorfor var han så livlig, så lykkelig, når han havde været oppe med solen, tilbragt hele morgenen i marken eller på tærskepladsen og nu kom hjem fra såning eller høslæt eller høst for at drikke te med hende? Hvorfor talte han med sådan en beundring og fryd om den dygtige og velstående bonde Matvej Jermisjin, der havde kørt korn ind med sin familie hele natten? Eller om, at hans egne, Nikolajs, neg stod i stak, før nogen anden havde fået høsten i hus? Hun forstod ikke, hvorfor han gik ud gennem vinduet til verandaen og smilede under overskægget og blinkede så fornøjet, når en lun, jævn regn faldt på den tørre, tørstige havres unge skud. Eller hvorfor han, når vinden drev en truende sky bort midt i høslættet, kom ind fra laden, rød, solbrændt og svedig, med duft af malurt og ensian i håret, gned hænderne af fryd og sagde: »Ja, én dag til, så har både bønderne og jeg alt vores korn under tag.«

Endnu mindre forstod hun, hvorfor han, der havde så godt et hjerte og altid kom hendes ønsker i forkøbet, kunne blive nær ved at fortvivle, når hun kom med en bøn fra en bonde eller bondekone, som havde bedt hende om at måtte slippe for noget arbejde. Hvorfor han, hendes gode Nikolaj, blev ved at sige nej og vredt bad hende holde sig fra det, der ikke kom hende ved. Hun mærkede, at han havde en verden for sig, som han elskede lidenskabeligt, og hvis love hun endnu ikke kendte.

Når hun af og til i et forsøg på at forstå ham talte om det gode, han gjorde for sine livegne, blev han vred og svarede: »Overhovedet ikke; det faldt mig aldrig ind, og det ville jeg ikke gøre for deres skyld! Alt det er poesi og kællingesnak — alt det med at gøre godt mod sin næste! Hvad jeg vil, er, at vores børn ikke skal være tiggere; jeg vil grundlægge vores families formue, og det er alt. Og for det kræves orden og strenghed. Det er sagen!« sagde han og knyttede sin blodrige næve. »Og retfærdighed selvfølgelig,« tilføjede han, »for hvis bonden er nøgen og sulten og kun har én ussel hest, kan han hverken gøre noget godt for sig selv eller for mig.«

Og alt, hvad Nikolaj foretog sig, bar frugt — formentlig netop fordi han nægtede at tillade sig at tro, at han gjorde godt mod andre for dydens skyld. Hans midler voksede hurtigt; livegne fra nabogodser kom for at bede ham om at købe dem, og længe efter hans død bevaredes mindet om hans styrelse med ærbødighed blandt bønderne. »Han var en rigtig herre!... Bøndernes sag først og så sin egen. Og slog ikke af på noget heller. Med ét ord: en rigtig herre!«

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: In the winter of 1813, Nicholas married Princess Mary and moved to Bald Hills with his wife, his mother, and Sonya.

Within four years he had paid off all his remaining debts without selling any of his wife's property, and having received a small inheritance from a deceased cousin, he repaid his debt to Pierre as well.
In another three years, by 1820, he had managed his affairs so well that he was able to buy a small estate adjoining Bald Hills and was in negotiations to buy back Otradnoe—his lifelong dream.

Having started farming out of necessity, Nicholas soon grew so devoted to it that it became his favorite—and nearly his only—occupation. He was a plain, practical farmer. He didn't like innovations, especially the English methods that were then coming into vogue. He laughed at theoretical treatises on agriculture, had no interest in factories in growing expensive crops or buying costly seed grain, and didn't obsess over any one part of his operation to the exclusion of the rest. What he always kept in mind was the estate as a whole, not any particular component. What mattered to him was not nitrogen in the soil or oxygen in the air, not special plows or fertilizers, but the principal instrument through which nitrogen, oxygen, plows, and fertilizers all worked—that is, the laboring peasant. When Nicholas first took up farming and began to understand its various branches, it was the peasant who especially engaged his attention. He saw the peasant not merely as a tool but as an end in himself and as a judge. At first he studied the peasant closely, trying to understand what he needed and what he considered good and bad, and only pretended to give orders while in fact learning from the peasants, their methods, and their language. Only when he understood the peasants' tastes and aspirations, had learned to speak their language and grasp the hidden meaning behind their words, and felt himself one of them, did he begin to manage them boldly—that is, to fulfill toward them the duty expected of him. And Nicholas’s management brought splendid results.

Guided by some intuitive gift, on taking over the estates he immediately appointed as bailiff, village elder, and delegate the very men the serfs would have chosen themselves if they'd had the right. And these appointments never changed. Before analyzing the chemical properties of manure, before exploring the principles of debit and credit (as he liked to mock), he calculated how many carts his peasants had and tried to increase their number; he kept the peasant families as large as possible and wouldn't allow them to split up; he was strict with the lazy, the vicious, and the weak, and tried to keep them out; and at sowing and harvest time he went out to the fields himself to oversee the work, studying the peasants' crops with the same attention he gave to his own.

He was as careful about the sowing and reaping of the peasants' hay and grain as his own, and few landowners had their crops sown and harvested as early, as well, or with as good a return as Nicholas.

He didn't like dealing with household serfs—the "drones," as he called them—and everyone said he spoiled them with his leniency. When a decision had to be made about a household serf, especially one who needed to be punished, he was always uncertain and consulted everyone in the house. But when it was possible to send a serf to serve as a soldier in place of a peasant, he did so without a moment's hesitation. He never felt the slightest uncertainty in his dealings with the peasants. He knew that every decision he made would be approved by all of them, with very rare exceptions.

He never let himself be harsh with someone or reward someone merely because he felt like it. He couldn't have said by what standard he measured what he should or shouldn't do, but the standard in his heart was firm and unwavering.
He would often speak with vexation about some failure or problem and say: "What can you do with our Russian peasants?" and imagine that he couldn't stand them.
Yet he loved "our Russian peasants" and their way of life with his whole soul, and for that very reason he had understood and adopted the one method of farming that produced good results.

Countess Mary was jealous of this passion of her husband's and regretted that she couldn't share it. But she couldn't grasp the joys and frustrations he drew from that world, so alien and remote to her. She couldn't understand why he was so particularly excited and happy when, having gotten up at dawn and spent the whole morning in the fields or on the threshing floor, he came back to tea from the sowing, mowing, or harvesting. She couldn't understand what made him so delighted when he talked enthusiastically about the prosperous, hardworking peasant Matthew Ermishin who had been up all night with his family carting sheaves, or about having gotten all his grain in before anyone else. She could not see why, when a steady, warm rain began to fall on the thirsty young oats, he would step through the window onto the veranda, smile under his mustache and wink in delight. Or why, when the wind carried off a threatening cloud during the hay harvest, he would come back from the barn flushed, sunburned and sweating, with the smell of wormwood and gentian in his hair, and rub his hands and say gleefully, “Well, another day and my grain and the peasants’ will all be under cover.”

Still less could she understand why, despite his kind heart and readiness to anticipate her wishes, he nearly lost his mind when she brought him a petition from some peasant men or women who had come to her asking to be excused from work—why he, a kind man, stubbornly refused, telling her angrily not to meddle in what was none of her business. She felt that he had a world entirely his own, which he loved passionately and which was governed by laws she did not understand.

Sometimes, when she tried to understand him and spoke of the good he was doing for his serfs, he would get annoyed and reply: "Not in the least; it never entered my head, and I wouldn't lift a finger for their good! That's all poetry and old wives' nonsense—all that doing good for one's neighbor! I don't want our children to go begging; I want to build up our family fortune while I'm alive. That's all. And to do that, you need order, you need discipline... That's the point!" he would say, clenching his large fist. "And fairness too, of course!" he would add. "Because if a peasant is naked and hungry and has only one wretched horse, he's no good to himself or to anyone else."

And probably because Nicholas allowed himself no thought of doing good for others for virtue's sake, everything he did was fruitful. His wealth grew rapidly; serfs from neighboring estates came begging him to buy them. And long after his death, the peasants preserved a devoted memory of his management. "He was a real master... The peasants' affairs first, then his own. And he didn't let you get away with anything. A real master!"
